# Cascadia Early Warning
::: {.cs-hook}
Every module before this one looked back. This one issues a number about next month, with a range, and then shows on a held-out period it was only allowed to run once whether numbers like it earned trust. 649,082 public device reports across seven product codes, frozen and hash-verified; a forecast pre-registered before the first row existed; and a review rule that opened one episode in 224 evaluated months, and says so.
:::
:::

[What volume should we expect next?](https://www.robbinsanalytics.com/cascadia-early-warning/){.btn .btn-primary}

---

## Overview

A quality organization is usually good at looking back and poorly equipped to look forward: where is reporting heading, and what is not a problem today but could be? This module supplies the forward-looking half with public data and without pretending to more than the data can carry.

It reads openFDA's device-event endpoint for seven Class III cardiovascular product codes (ventricular assist devices, percutaneous circulatory support, transcatheter aortic valves, implantable defibrillator and resynchronization generators and leads, and intra-aortic balloon pumps), counts one report per code per receipt month, and issues a one-month-ahead forecast with 50% and 80% ranges. A fixed candidate model is tested against two naive baselines on a development period, promoted per code only where it beats the better baseline by at least ten percent, and then run **once** on a locked held-out period of 24 months whose scores are published as they came out. A pre-registered review rule turns months that depart from expectation into a human review queue.

The page says what the forecast is and what it is not. A report count is not an incident rate, an event rate, or a measure of device safety; FDA says so in as many words and the page quotes it. No manufacturer or brand is named anywhere, by decision, and the exclusion that keeps the module at arm's length from any one firm is applied by a private token list with a public receipt.

---

## Why This Stack

The source is public and keyless, the series are small, and the discipline is in the chronology rather than the compute. So: Python freezes 729 API responses and asserts the freeze by SHA-256 (the record-level payloads carry narratives and addresses and run to hundreds of megabytes, so the staging files are gitignored and the manifest is what is committed, the same departure Matter Ledger recorded); **DuckDB** holds the record grain and re-derives every published cell down a second path written in SQL; **statsmodels** fits the one candidate form, an ETS model with damped trend and twelve-month seasonality on log counts, from which the final states are exported so an independent recurrence can recompute every point; and the page is static HTML with Apache ECharts, every figure computed at build time from the committed tables.

The chrome is the portfolio's own design system by pointer, not copy, and the charts follow the visualization standard gated by its chart review, including the blind reading panel.

---

## Architecture

**openFDA device event (count series and record-level pages, frozen by hash) → DuckDB record grain and committed monthly tables → forecast harness fixed in `config/model.json` → scores, review queue and recall context → static ECharts page.
A weekly live edge re-reads the count series, keeps each week's view as a vintage, scores each issued forecast as its month elapses, and never publishes.**

- **Freeze.** Every request, its retrieval time, the API's own `last_updated` and a SHA-256 per response are in the source register. The count series are committed outright; the record-level pages are asserted by hash and recomputed by the validator on every run.
- **Exclude.** Reports whose manufacturer fields match a private list are removed whole. The list is never committed; its SHA-256, the derived set of 671 excluded product codes and a receipt of counts per field are. It removed one report of 649,083.
- **Model.** One count definition, one `mdr_report_key` per code per receipt month. The harness, the periods, the interval method and the promotion rule were committed before the first forecast row existed; the git log is the proof.
- **Test.** Development targets 2022 to 2023 chose the model per code. The locked test, 2024-01 to 2025-12, ran once, from origins at or after 2023-12, and its scores were not revisited. The validator checks both facts from the commit history.
- **Review.** A month is flagged when its actual exceeds the 80% upper range by five or more reports; two consecutive flags open an episode. The rule is disabled for a code whose locked-test coverage fell below 70%, and three codes are shown with it off.
- **Operate.** A scheduled task, seven keyless calls a week, re-reads the series and reconciles against the frozen snapshot; a hook refuses any commit or push from an unattended run.

---

## Headline Skill: A forecast you are allowed to be wrong about, in public

The differentiator is not the model, which is deliberately plain. It is that **everything that could flatter the result was decided before the result existed, and the result is published as it came out.**

- **Pre-registered.** The harness, the chance rate the review rule would produce on noise, the one count definition, the known-answer check and the scope cuts were written down and committed before any forecast row.
- **Locked, once.** The held-out period was run a single time. The validator reads the git history and fails if a locked row has ever changed or if the promotion decision was committed after the first locked row.
- **Honest ranges.** The 80% ranges covered between 33% and 100% of locked months across the seven codes. Two codes were inside the pre-registered band, two above it and three below the line that disables the rule. The page shows all seven and the numbers gate records that the build continued under its own rule rather than quietly tuning.
- **Honest latency.** Data through 2026-08-31, retrieved 2026-10-06. A September figure issued in October is labelled an elapsed-period estimate, not a forecast.
- **Context, not validation.** FDA's Class I recall record for these codes is drawn beside the review queue: 24 initiations in the evaluated span, none preceded by an episode start. The page says that is association only, and the shuffled-dates test that could make it more is recorded as the next build, not claimed.

---

## Validation

**Nothing publishes unless a second, independently written path agrees.** A hand-computed golden fixture of 23 rows was committed before either engine existed, and both engines reproduce it. The independent path streams the staged pages into DuckDB and recomputes every published cell in SQL, with the exclusion re-implemented as SQL macros rather than the build's Python; **10,598 of 10,598 cells reconcile.** The domain gate runs fourteen checks, from the freeze hashes to the known-answer recovery, and then **proves each one can fail** by corrupting a copy and confirming the check trips.

The charts were read by a **blind four-seat reading panel**: three domain seats cast from the decision the page serves (a post-market surveillance manager, a forecast back-test reviewer, and a quality-systems director who is not an analyst) plus a canvas-only visualization reader. It returned 41 findings and 30 defects, of which 27 were fixed before anything shipped; four of four seats independently found that months flagged in lanes where the rule is off read as live episodes, which the author had not written down.

---

## The Module

One page, read top to bottom, arguing one thing.

- **The outlook.** For the headline code: expect about 672 reports in September 2026, with an 80% range of 329 to 838, drawn as twenty outcomes from the model's own error history rather than a bare point.
- **The locked test.** Twenty-four months the model never saw. The candidate's range held 22 of them; its average miss was 246 reports a month against the trailing mean's 265, which is the honest size of the improvement.
- **Did the ranges hold.** Coverage by code, against the nominal 80%, the pre-registered band and the 70% line that switches the rule off.
- **What deserves review.** One lane per code: flagged months, the one episode, and the Class I recall initiations drawn beside them as context.
- **How complete is the recent record.** Reports by the month the event happened, counted within three, six and twelve months, so that like is compared with like and the most recent months are shown as filling rather than falling.

---

## Roadmap

- The shuffled-dates null: re-run the recall count against event dates shuffled within code, so the one pre-registered count has a reference distribution.
- A record-level live edge with the exclusion applied, so live months and frozen months share one basis.
- An openFDA API key, which raises the daily budget and lets the freeze refresh in one session.

## Disclosure

Built from public FDA data: the openFDA device event, recall, enforcement and classification endpoints, frozen at receipts through 2026-08-31 and verified by SHA-256. **No client data and no proprietary data of any kind.**

The module is aggregate by construction: report counts per product code per month. It names no manufacturer or brand, publishes no rate and no risk, and presents no count, forecast or review flag as a statement about the safety of any device. FDA's own caution applies and is quoted on the page: these reports are unverified, may be incomplete or duplicated, and cannot be used to estimate the incidence of an event.

Independent portfolio project. Nothing here is regulatory or medical advice.
